docs.title: Home
docs.text:
This is the homepage for HandyUI documentation.

You will get introduced to HandyUI and the reason to it's existence here.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Code-only (like WinForms)
  • Uses SkiaSharp for rendering
  • Open Source and free to modify (MIT license)

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
Basically, I (davpnuser) was trying to make a modern, hardware-accelerated GUI app in C# and modern .NET. I tried using WinForms, Uses GDI+. What about WPF? Uses XAML. Well, what about Avalonia? Nope, it has a lot of boilerplate. WinUI Markup? Sucks.

So, i was basically trying to find a option that didnt exist so at one point i got tired and started using SkiaSharp with WinForms. (yes, i know, i was using the exact framework i didnt use at first.) And it was going good until... I realized that WinForms is NOT cross-platform. So, i decided to try using alternatives such as OpenTK's C# library and Silk.NET and etc.

But, ultimately, i found that Silk.NET works best. So, i was then using pure Silk.NET and SkiaSharp for a while until i realized once again, that, there was a lot of boilerplate. So, i began work on HandyUI. At first, it was really incapable. Really. Incapable. Then, over time, it started getting better with more and more updates.

My decision of seperating the core renderer to a seperate library especially helped me out when i wanted to make a Silk.NET adapter. I first made the Silk.NET adapter, and once it got stable enough, i deprecated the WinForms (legacy) adapter.

docs.title: What's next for HandyUI?
docs.text: I can't tell. It has way more features than it used to have, but still, im a solo developer. Don't expect much advanced work from me. I'm a human too, after all. Still, i will be maintaining this package as long as i physically can until i either get burnt out or i take a break. But, you should not expect advanced built-in controls from me. That is your work. You can use a control library; Make a control library. Do what you want but dont expect advanced controls from me.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
HandyUI is split across three packages. Each layer builds on the one below.

Package Purpose HandyUI.Core Renderer, controls base, modules, theming, animation, helpers. HandyUI.Controls Ready-made controls built on Core. HandyUI.SilkNet GLFW-backed host window and Win32 integrations.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public sealed class ClickBox : BaseControl<ClickBox>
{
    public ClickBox() { Focusable = true; }

    public event Action? WhenClicked;

    public override bool DoesIntersect(SKPoint point) => Bounds.Contains(point);

    public override void OnDraw(SKCanvas canvas)
    {
        using var paint = new SKPaint
        {
            Color = IsHovered ? SKColors.Orange : SKColors.CornflowerBlue
        };
        canvas.DrawRect(Bounds, paint);
    }

    protected override bool OnMouse(MouseEventContext eventContext)
    {
        if (eventContext.Type != MouseEventType.ClickEvent) return false;
        WhenClicked?.Invoke();
        return true;
    }
}

docs.title: Input Contexts
docs.text:
HandyUI.Core.Data.MouseEventContext and KeyEventContext.

Both are readonly record struct and carry a reference to the current TweenManager. Controls that need to start a tween from inside OnMouse / OnKey can use eventContext.TweenManager directly:

protected override bool OnMouse(MouseEventContext eventContext)
{
    if (eventContext.Type != MouseEventType.MouseDownEvent) return false;
    eventContext.TweenManager.To(0f, 1f, 0.3f, v => Animate(v));
    return true;
}

docs.title: MouseEventContext
docs.text:
public readonly record struct MouseEventContext(
    TweenManager TweenManager,
    SKPoint? MousePosition,
    MouseEventType Type = MouseEventType.None,
    MouseButton Button = MouseButton.None,
    int WheelDelta = 0,
    int ClickCount = 1,
    bool IsControlPressed = false,
    bool IsShiftPressed = false,
    bool IsAltPressed = false
);
Field Meaning TweenManager Current animation engine. MousePosition Local cursor position, or null when the subtree is clipped. Type See MouseEventType. Button Which button triggered the event. WheelDelta Wheel delta in clicks (±120 per notch). ClickCount 1, 2 (double), or 3 (triple) - computed by the adapter from timing + distance. Modifiers State at event time.

Null means clipped

MousePosition is null - not a sentinel coordinate - when the control is outside its clip region. BaseControl.IsHovered uses MousePosition != null && Bounds.Contains(pos).

Synthesized clicks

MouseEventType.ClickEvent is never sent by the adapter. It is synthesized by UIRenderer.ProcessMouseEvent after a MouseUpEvent that occurs on the currently pressed control. Custom controls should listen for ClickEvent (not MouseUpEvent) when they want click-detection.

docs.title: KeyEventContext
docs.text:
public readonly record struct KeyEventContext(
    TweenManager Tweener,
    KeyEventType Type = KeyEventType.None,
    int? KeyCode = null,
    char Character = '\0',
    bool IsControlPressed = false,
    bool IsShiftPressed = false,
    bool IsAltPressed = false
);
Field Meaning Tweener Current animation engine. Type KeyDown, KeyUp, or CharInput. KeyCode Virtual key code. null for CharInput. Character Printable character for CharInput.

KeyCode is nullable

KeyCode is int? so CharInput events can skip it. When working with KeyEventType.KeyDown / KeyUp, cast or pattern-match before comparing: if (ctx.KeyCode == 8) { ... } still works because int? compares to int implicitly.

docs.title: HandyWindow
docs.text:
HandyUI.SilkNet.Components.HandyWindow

Silk.NET / GLFW implementation of IHostWindow. Owns the pump thread, GL context bridge, Win32 integrations, custom title-bar handling, drag logic, DPI, and tray icon.

public class HandyWindow : IDisposable, IHostWindow

Windows only

Construction throws PlatformNotSupportedException on non-Windows platforms.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
public HandyWindow(WindowConfiguration windowConfiguration);

The constructor calls ThemeHelper.EnsureInitialized() and spins up the pump thread.

var window = new HandyWindow(WindowConfiguration.Default with { Title = "Chat" });
var renderer = RendererHelper.Attach(window);
window.Run();

docs.title: IHostWindow implementation
docs.text:
All IHostWindow members are implemented, with these notable additions:

Member Notes Title Mirrors InternalWindow.Title. Icon Deferred apply - set then pumped onto the pump thread after init. Size Returns SKSize.Empty until initialized. UseDirtyRendering Mirrors InternalWindow.IsEventDriven. VSync Pass-through. FramesPerSecond Stored property; used when VSync is off. Cursor Deferred apply on the pump thread via RendererAdapter.SetCursor. IsForeground True while window has focus. DeviceType Always Desktop. Orientation Landscape / portrait; updated on resize. DpiScale GetDeviceCaps(LOGPIXELSX) / 96. DisplayDist Physical diagonal in inches (via HORZSIZE / VERTSIZE). 0 if unknown. TweenManager Assigned by UIRenderer. Renderer The attached UIRenderer, or null. TotalTime Mirrors Renderer.TotalTime. WhenOrientationChanged Raised on landscape ↔ portrait flips. Invalidate() Wakes the pump thread and raises WhenInvalidated.

docs.title: Drag with DragRegions
docs.text:
The idiomatic custom-title-bar pattern:

window.IsTitleBarVisible = false;
window.Border = WindowBorder.Resizable;

// Tell HandyWindow that the top 40 px of the client area behaves like a title bar.
window.DragRegions.Add(new SKRect(0, 0, window.Size.Width, 40));

window.WhenResized += size =>
{
    window.DragRegions.Clear();
    window.DragRegions.Add(new SKRect(0, 0, size.Width, 40));
};

Now mouse-downs in the top 40 px are routed to the OS HTCAPTION behavior automatically - the WndProc handles it via WM_NCHITTEST.

Focusable

Setting Focusable = true is required before RequestFocus() or Tab navigation will target the control. Clicking a Focusable control sets focus automatically; clicking a non-focusable one clears it.

docs.text:
HandyUI.Core.Abstractions.Interface.IModule

Contract for logic-only components. Modules run before controls in the input pipeline - but they cannot consume events. Their input handlers are purely observational: a module always sees the event, and processing always continues to the controls below.

public interface IModule : IDisposable

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
string? Name         { get; set; }
bool    AcceptsInput { get; set; }   // default: true
bool    Enabled      { get; set; }   // default: true
bool    IsDisposed   { get; }

docs.title: AcceptsInput
docs.text:
When false, UIRenderer skips the module during the input pipeline. The module still ticks in UpdateModules. Set this on modules that only animate.

Modules cannot consume input

ProcessMouseEvent and ProcessKeyEvent return void in v4. A module observes input but always lets it fall through to the controls. If you need a component that can consume input, use a control (IControl) or handle the event through a focused control.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
abstract void OnUpdate(UpdateContext updateContext);

void Start();   // Enabled = true, calls OnStart()
void Stop();    // Enabled = false, calls OnStop()

void ProcessMouseEvent(MouseEventContext eventContext);
void ProcessKeyEvent(KeyEventContext eventContext);

ProcessMouseEvent / ProcessKeyEvent are no-ops when Enabled is false or AcceptsInput is false.

public void ProcessMouseEvent(MouseEventContext eventContext)
{
    if (Enabled) OnMouse(eventContext);
}

public void ProcessKeyEvent(KeyEventContext eventContext)
{
    if (Enabled) OnKey(eventContext);
}

docs.title: ProfilerControl
docs.text:
HandyUI.Core.Helpers.Controls.ProfilerControl

Internal

ProfilerControl is internal. You cannot construct it directly. It is created automatically by UIRenderer in Debug builds when UseProfiler is true, and toggled at runtime with Ctrl+Shift+G.

The profiler overlay displays:

  • FPS + target FPS
  • V-Sync / Dirty Rendering / Foreground state
  • Current cursor type
  • Managed memory (MB), GC counts (gen 0/½)
  • Total elapsed seconds
  • A 200-frame frame-time graph with target-FPS line

docs.title: Interactive buttons
docs.text:
Button Effect Toggle DiRe Toggles Host.UseDirtyRendering. Toggle V-Sync Toggles Host.VSync. Inc. Target FPS Host.FramesPerSecond += 5. Dec. Target FPS Host.FramesPerSecond -= 5.

The profiler control is registered with ZIndex = 10000, so it always renders above every other control on the renderer. Its top-left position is (0, 0) in the client area.

docs.title: Enabling programmatically
docs.text:
renderer.UseProfiler = true;

Enabling creates the control; disabling destroys and disposes it.

public double TotalTime { get; }

Total elapsed seconds since the UIRenderer was constructed. Backed by a Stopwatch that starts immediately and is not reset - it advances even while dirty rendering skips paint frames. This makes it suitable for long-running animations or session timers.

Wall-clock time, not tick time

Earlier versions accumulated TotalTime only inside UpdateModules. The current implementation uses a monotonic Stopwatch, so TotalTime keeps ticking during idle frames of the dirty renderer.

public bool KeyboardFocus { get; set; } = false;

Whether the renderer treats Tab / Shift+Tab as focus-cycling shortcuts. When false (the default), Tab is delivered to the focused control (or modules) just like any other key. Set KeyboardFocus = true to enable keyboard navigation:

Why it's opt-in

Many apps want Tab to mean "insert a tab character" (e.g. code editors with a focused MultilineTextInput). Leaving KeyboardFocus = false by default lets apps keep the standard tab-in-text behavior. Toggle it when the user enters a form or navigation context.

public void FocusNext();

Cycles focus through Focusable controls in ZIndex order. Called automatically by ProcessKeyEvent on Tab (Shift+Tab = previous).

docs.title: ProcessMouseEvent(MouseEventContext)
docs.text:
public void ProcessMouseEvent(MouseEventContext context);
  1. Returns early if context.MousePosition == null.
  2. Processes pending controls.
  3. Runs the module input pipeline. Modules observe each event but cannot consume it - the pipeline always continues to the controls below.
  4. Hit-tests controls (highest ZIndex first).
  5. On MouseDownEvent: tracks _pressedControl and sets or clears focus.
  6. Dispatches recursively into the tree.
  7. On MouseUpEvent: synthesizes a ClickEvent to _pressedControl if it's still under the cursor.

docs.title: ProcessKeyEvent(KeyEventContext)
docs.text:
public bool ProcessKeyEvent(KeyEventContext context);
  1. Ctrl+Shift+G toggles the profiler (Debug builds).
  2. Runs the module input pipeline (observe-only).
  3. Forwards to the focused control.
  4. If KeyboardFocus is true and the key is Tab:
  5. Shift+Tab → FocusPrevious()
  6. Tab → FocusNext()
  7. Returns true if any step handled the event; otherwise false.

Modules cannot consume input

Unlike controls, modules never block propagation. Their ProcessMouseEvent / ProcessKeyEvent return void, so every event reaches both modules and controls. If you need a component that can swallow input, use an IControl with Focusable = true (for keys) or a control whose OnMouse returns true.

docs.title: Focus rectangles
docs.text: When focus was set by keyboard (FocusNext / Tab), the renderer draws a focus rectangle on the focused control after its subtree. Clicking a control switches to non-keyboard focus and the rectangle disappears.

docs.title: Synthetic events on focus change
docs.text:
When the focused control changes, SetFocus dispatches two synthetic MoveEvents to keep IsHovered responsive:

Target MousePosition Effect Old focused control null IsHovered → false (blur) New focused control SKPoint.Empty IsHovered → Bounds.Contains(0, 0)

The events are typed MoveEvent purely as a state-ping - no press or click logic fires. Controls can override OnMouse to react to focus state changes if they need to.

Why this exists

Without it, a control losing focus could keep rendering its hover highlight if the cursor happened to still be over it. Sending a null move clears that state deterministically.

docs.title: Dirty rendering
docs.text: Two-frame invalidation. RenderControls early-outs when host.UseDirtyRendering is true and the frame counter is ≤ 0.

docs.title: Module pipeline
docs.text:
Modules do not get input by default. To participate in input, they must have AcceptsInput = true (default)

Modules also cant consume inputs.

docs.title: Profiler overlay
docs.text: When UseProfiler = true, a ProfilerControl is created on the first render and assigned ZIndex = 10000 so it renders on top of every other control.

docs.text:
All controls derive from BaseControl<TSelf> and live in the HandyUI.Controls package, under HandyUI.Controls.Controls. Controls-specific enums are in HandyUI.Controls.Enums.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Autosizing - each control runs ResizeToContent() in its constructor and whenever a relevant property changes. Leave Width and Height at their defaults (usually 0) to auto-size.
  • Theming - controls read colors from ThemeManager at draw time, so changing the OS theme recolors everything live.
  • Events - every callback event is named WhenXxx; each has a fluent WithWhenXxx(...) helper (e.g. WithWhenClicked, WithWhenToggled).
  • Animation - hover / ripple / focus / checkmark animations use TweenManager via UpdateContext.TweenManager (in OnUpdate) or MouseEventContext.TweenManager (in OnMouse). If the tween manager is missing (a null Tween), values snap to their target.
  • Focus - text inputs and toggles call RequestFocus() and rely on Focusable = true. Most display controls leave Focusable = false.
  • Disposal - every control disposes its paints and typeface in OnDispose().

docs.text:
In this guide, i will be teaching how to make a custom HandyUI control and will be giving some custom control examples.

Prerequisites

First of all, you will need a .NET 10 project preferably using C#. Second of all, you will need to have HandyUI installed on your .NET project. (How you can do that)

docs.title: Anatomy of a HandyUI Control
docs.text:
Since HandyUI operates as a retained UI Framework without an layout engine, every custom control you build is responsible for three things:

  • 1: State: Holding its own properties and turning unnecessary public properties into fields.

  • 2: Rendering: Drawing itself, relative to its current state.

  • 3: Input: Handling input events and consuming a input event when required.

docs.title: Step-by-Step: Building a custom Toggle Switch
docs.text: Let's build a simple and interactive ToggleSwitch control from scratch.

docs.title: Step 1: Define the control and it's properties.
docs.text:
We will start by creating a new C# file called ToggleSwitch.cs. You do not particularly need to name it ToggleSwitch.cs but we will use this as a placeholder for this guide.

Then, you will define a class inside the new ToggleSwitch.cs file we just created.

Here's what i have created for this guide:

public class ToggleSwitch
{
    // Empty.
}

After that, you can define the control class's properties.

Here's what we will add:

public class ToggleSwitch
{
    public bool Checked { get; private set; }
    public event Action<bool>? WhenToggled;
}
Now, here comes an important part.

We will make our newly created class inherit from BaseControl.

Here's how you can do that:

public class ToggleSwitch : BaseControl<ToggleSwitch>
{
    public bool Checked { get; private set; }
    public event Action<bool>? WhenToggled;

    public override void OnDraw(SKCanvas canvas)
    {
        // No drawing code yet.
    }

    public override bool DoesIntersect(SKPoint point)
    {
        return Bounds.Contains(point);
    }
}
Well, you might now be asking "What does DoesIntersect do and why did you inherit from BaseControl<ToggleSwitch> and not just BaseControl directly?"

About the BaseControl<ToggleSwitch> one:

Well, you can always just use normal BaseControl BUT keep in mind that you can't use the fluent APIs on your control if you dont inherit like that.

It's called CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) in programming terms and it basically lets the fluent APIs return your control as your control's type instead of converting it into a generic BaseControl.

docs.title: Debugging a HandyUI app
docs.text:
You can debug a HandyUI app in three ways:

  • Using a proper debugger and compiling in Debug mode. (an example would be the VS2026 debugger.)

or

  • Using the built-in profiler for simpler debugging.

or

  • Using both methods (recommended)

docs.title: Using a proper debugger
docs.text:
You don't have to go through any hoops in order to debug your HandyUI app.

HandyUI most of the time works without any issues in debugging environments.

Recommendations for your debugger

I heavily recommend that you enable Just My Code in your debugger settings so that you dont have to step through the internal HandyUI library code when you are debugging a app that uses HandyUI.

docs.title: Using the built-in profiler
docs.text:
Prerequisites

You will need to either compile your app in Debug mode or enable the profiler via doing renderer.UseProfiler = true in code before compiling.

Opening the profiler

To open the profiler on a HandyUI app that has the profiler enabled, you can press Ctrl+Shift+G.

docs.title: What you can do with the HandyUI profiler
docs.text:
• You can see the current app rendering FPS and target FPS.
  • You can see whether V-Sync and dirty rendering (AKA DiRe internally.) is turned on.
  • You can see whether the app is currently focused or not.
  • You can see what cursor is currently being shown by controls.
  • You can see the app managed memory usage.
  • You can see the total generation 0/1/2 GC amounts.
  • You can see the app runtime length.
  • You can spot frame timing issues using the frametime graph.
  • You can toggle dirty rendering (AKA DiRe internally.), and V-Sync on and off.
  • You can increase/decrease the app's target FPS.

docs.title: Using both methods
docs.text:
The Recommended Debugging Workflow:

  • 1: Run your app and press Ctrl+Shift+G to spot performance bottlenecks or stuttering frames using the profiler.
  • 2: Once you identify that a specific view or component is causing a frame spike, switch to your IDE debugger.
  • 3: Set a conditional breakpoint inside that component's logic to isolate the root cause and inspect why the state update or render cycle took longer than expected.
